catalog_quote: 2.1. Simple stems are always monosyllabic in GHZ. Compound stems tend to be bisyllabic, but it is not always possible to determine the meaning of both of the syllable, although the second syllable is usually recognizable. The reason for this is that there is a general rule of neutralization in GHZ which simplifies the syllable nucleus of all prestressed syllables. Tones are neutralized to high tone in prestressed syllables across morpheme boundaries (e.g., in compounds). ... Another type of compounding is that of the verb stem plus the morpheme -nǒ Acompaniment/Instrument or a stative verb stem such as -yǎʔnʸ young, which modify the meaning of the verb stem. In these compounds also the first element loses its stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress sits on the verb/noun stem (root): simple stems are monosyllabic and stressed; in compound stems the final element carries the stress and all preceding ('prestressed') syllables are unstressed and undergo nucleus and tone neutralization; aspect prefixes precede the stressed stem; syllabic person enclitics after the stem bear only secondary stress. I.e. stress on the last syllable of the (compound) stem = root stress, not counted from a word edge. This is inferred from Marks's usage, not from an explicit stress rule; the paper has no prosody section.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Syllabic person enclitics (-á?, -í?, -ú, -mè, -yáhk etc.) are described as 'secondarily stressed syllables' (p.81); -yáhk is said to occur 'in a non-final, secondarily stressed syllable' (p.82).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; first elements of compounds (including verb + -nǒ accompaniment/instrument or stative stem) lose stress to the final element.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the verb word (aspect prefix + stem + enclitics) and noun compounds; tone (high, low, rising) and nucleus types (V, V?, Vh) are contrastive only in stressed and secondarily stressed syllables per the neutralization rule. No explicit statement of the form 'stress falls on X'; a fuller treatment presumably exists in Marks 1978 ms and Benn 2021.
new_statements.identity_note: Marks 1980 describes Guevea de Humboldt Zapotec proper ('GHZ', town of Guevea de Humboldt, Isthmus of Tehuantepec; = zpg/guev1238). Benn 2016/2021 describe the Santa María Guienagati variety, which Benn groups with Guevea and Petapa (zpf, peta1247) as 'Northeast Tehuantepec Zapotec'; Glottolog attaches Benn 2021 to guev1238, though Guienagati is sometimes associated with Lachiguiri Zapotec (zpa, lach1250). The quoted statement is from the Guevea variety itself.

sources.note: No dedicated stress section (fn.1 gives only segments, V?/Vh nucleus types and three tones), but stress is presupposed as stem-based: simple stems are monosyllabic; in compounds all 'prestressed syllables' undergo nucleus/tone neutralization and 'the first element loses its stress'; morphophonemic rules 'affect only the stressed (final) syllable of a compound verb stem' (pp.51-52); syllabic person enclitics 'are secondarily stressed syllables' (p.81), -yahk 3pl occurs 'in a non-final, secondarily stressed syllable' (p.82). Aspect prefixes carry no stress discussion (they precede the stem).

sources.citation: Benn, Joshua. 2016. Consonant-Tone-Phonation Interactions in Guienagati Zapotec. Proc. TAL 2016 (Buffalo), 125-128. doi:10.21437/TAL.2016-27
sources.note: Silent on stress. Describes (C)V and (C)VC roots (historical V2 lost), ~60 consonants with a three-way coda contrast, L/M/H tone on modal vowels, checked vs rearticulated glottalized vowels; notes roots and pronominal enclitics carry contrastive tone/phonation while prefixes do not. Variety: Santa María Guienagati (sister of Guevea and Petapa within NETZ).
